```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
## The evaluation harness runs on optional packages, so its chunks are skipped without them
has_stack <- all(vapply(c("mlr3", "mlr3proba", "mlr3extralearners", "glmnet", "praznik", "stabm"),
                        requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE))
```

`survfcbf` carries the fast correlation-based filter (FCBF, Yu and Liu 2003) to right-censored
outcomes. It keeps a small panel of features in which no feature is made redundant by a more
relevant one, using an approximate Markov blanket. This vignette selects a panel from a simulated
dataset, inspects the decisions behind it, scores it against the known truth, and evaluates it
without information leakage.

Use it when a compact, non-redundant panel is what you need. If you need the best discrimination
whatever the panel size, or a ranking that stays stable under resampling, the rankers the package
wraps do better on real expression data.

```{r}
library(survfcbf)
```

## A dataset with known truth

`simulate_dataset()` generates block-correlated features whose roles are recorded in a manifest:
driver clusters with redundant members, correlated distractors, and noise. Because the truth is
known, a selection can be scored.

```{r}
sim <- simulate_dataset(default_params(
  p = 300L, n = 400L, k_drivers = 3L, cluster_size = 5L,
  n_distractor_subblocks = 2L, distractor_size = 8L,
  censor_fraction = 0.5, target_C = 0.75,
  seed = 1L, calib_n_presample = 800L
))
sim$realized$n_events
table(sim$manifest$role)
```

## Selecting a panel

The recommended mode fixes the panel size with `top`. Relevance and pruning run as usual until
that many predominant features are kept, so the result is deterministic and needs no permutations.

```{r}
sel <- survfcbf_select(sim$time, sim$status, sim$X, q = 2L, top = 5L)
sel$selected
```

`q` is the number of equal-frequency bins. Left at `NULL` it follows Bommert's rule, which gives 10
here. The benchmark reported for the package runs this mode at `q = 2`, so set it explicitly to
reproduce that configuration.

The indices point into the columns of `X`. On this dataset the panel holds three members of the
driver clusters and two noise features, because `top` asks for more features than there are signals:

```{r}
sim$manifest$role[sel$selected]
```

## Inspecting the decisions

Everything the filter decided is kept in `sel$trace`. `removed` lists each pruned feature, the
feature that made it redundant, and the two values of symmetrical uncertainty that were compared.
A feature goes when it is more strongly tied to its blanket than to the target.

```{r}
head(sel$trace$removed, 3)
```

`representative_per_cluster` gives the group each selected feature stands for:

```{r}
sel$trace$representative_per_cluster[1:2]
```

## Scoring against the truth

Members of a driver cluster are interchangeable, so recovery is scored by cluster rather than by
exact index. A cluster counts as found when any of its members is selected.

```{r}
unlist(score_selection_clusterwise(sel$selected, sim$manifest)[c("sensitivity", "fdr", "exact_recovery")])
```

## The permutation mode

Without `top` the filter chooses its own panel size: relevance is thresholded at a value `delta`
taken from a permutation null of the target. This is the original formulation, but with few events
the threshold can exceed the relevance of the true signals, and the panel comes back very small or
empty. A panel of fewer than two features is also too small for a penalised Cox model downstream.

```{r}
pm <- survfcbf_select(sim$time, sim$status, sim$X, B = 50L, seed = 1L)
pm$delta
length(pm$selected)
```

That is why `top` is the recommended mode.

## Evaluating without leakage

`benchmark_selectors()` runs selectors through nested cross-validation on an `mlr3proba` task.
Everything learned from data is fitted on the training fold only. This part needs the optional
packages listed in the README. The call below uses 3 folds to stay quick, so its numbers illustrate
the output and say nothing about the methods.

```{r, eval = has_stack, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(mlr3)
library(mlr3proba)
library(mlr3extralearners)
lgr::get_logger("mlr3")$set_threshold("warn")

task <- surv_task(sim$time, sim$status, sim$X)
selectors <- default_selectors(prop = 0.1, topk = 5L)[c("survfcbf_topk", "variance", "mim_surv")]
learner <- lrn("surv.cv_glmnet", alpha = 0, s = "lambda.min")

results <- benchmark_selectors(task, selectors, learner, outer_folds = 3L, seed = 1L)
results[, c("selector", "uno_c_trunc", "uno_c", "ibs", "stability", "parsimony", "n_failed", "n_null_fit")]
```

`uno_c_trunc` is the primary discrimination metric: Uno's C truncated at the 80th percentile of
the follow-up of each training fold (the `truncation` argument). The untruncated `uno_c` is kept for
comparison. Its censoring weights grow without bound for test events beyond the last censoring time
of the training fold, so a few pairs can decide the value of a fold.

Two more columns deserve attention:

- `n_failed` counts folds where no model could be fitted, usually because the panel was too small.
- `n_null_fit` counts folds where the learner ignored its features and predicted the baseline. Keep
  `s = "lambda.min"` in the ridge Cox learner. At its default `lambda.1se`, with far more features
  than events, the learner collapses to the null model, and every panel then gets the same
  integrated Brier score. It can still happen under `lambda.min` when a panel carries no signal. A
  non-zero count means those folds do not measure the selected panel.

Compare selectors at the same panel size where you can. In the call above the rankers keep 10% of
the features against 5 for `survfcbf_topk`, so the table measures panel size as well as the
selection rule.
